text:
Court of King’s Bench of Alberta

Citation: Sabbah v Sabbah, 2024 ABKB 758

Date:
20241218

Docket:
4803 195956

Registry:
Edmonton

Between:

Shannon Sabbah

Applicant

- and -

Eli Sabbah

Respondent

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Decision

of the

Honourable Justice

Peter Michalyshyn

_______________________________________________________

Introduction

[
1
]

The applicant Shannon Sabbah seeks an order striking the pleadings of the respondent Eli Sabbah and prohibiting any further applications in the action until such time that he agrees to give Ms Sabbah a religious divorce in Judaism, known as a Get. For reasons which follow, the application is allowed.

Background

[
2
]

The parties were married on December 10, 2012 and separated on September 3, 2020. Ms Sabbah requested a Get on May 4, 2021. She brought the within application on March 1, 2024. Mr. Sabbah argues he is unable to give Ms Sabbah a Get until he and his wife are civilly divorced. He says his refusal is “in accordance with his deeply held religious beliefs”. He says that once the civil divorce is granted, he will provide the Get.

The Law

[
3
]

Pursuant to
s. 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
, the Court has discretion to refuse to hear a party who fails to eliminate barriers to the remarriage of a spouse entitled to a divorce in Canada.  The process for exercising that discretion is as follows:

Affidavit re removal of barriers to religious remarriage

(2) In any proceedings under this Act, a spouse (in this section referred to as the “deponent”) may serve on the other spouse and file with the court an affidavit indicating

(a) that the other spouse is the spouse of the deponent;

(b) the date and place of the marriage, and the official character of the person who solemnized the marriage;

(c) the nature of any barriers to the remarriage of the deponent within the deponent’s religion the removal of which is within the other spouse’s control;

(d) where there are any barriers to the remarriage of the other spouse within the other spouse’s religion the removal of which is within the deponent’s control, that the deponent

(i) has removed those barriers, and the date and circumstances of that removal, or

(ii) has signified a willingness to remove those barriers, and the date and circumstances of that signification;

(e) that the deponent has, in writing, requested the other spouse to remove all of the barriers to the remarriage of the deponent within the deponent’s religion the removal of which is within the other spouse’s control;

(f) the date of the request described in paragraph (e); and

(g) that the other spouse, despite the request described in paragraph (e), has failed to remove all of the barriers referred to in that paragraph.

Powers of court where barriers not removed

(3) Where a spouse who has been served with an affidavit under subsection (2) does not

(a) within fifteen days after that affidavit is filed with the court or within such longer period as the court allows, serve on the deponent and file with the court an affidavit indicating that all of the barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e) have been removed, and

(b) satisfy the court, in any additional manner that the court may require, that all of the barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e) have been removed,

the court may, subject to any terms that the court considers appropriate,

(c) dismiss any application filed by that spouse under this Act, and

(d) strike out any other pleadings and affidavits filed by that spouse under this Act.

Special case

(4) Without limiting the generality of the court’s discretion under subsection (3), the court may refuse to exercise its powers under paragraphs (3)(c) and (d) where a spouse who has been served with an affidavit under subsection (2)

(a) within fifteen days after that affidavit is filed with the court or within such longer period as the court allows, serves on the deponent and files with the court an affidavit indicating genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e); and

(b) satisfies the court, in any additional manner that the court may require, that the spouse has genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e).

[
4
]

Ms. Sabbah has complied with the s 21.1(2) procedure triggering this court’s consideration of s 21.1 relief.

[
5
]

The issues to be decided on this application are therefore, (a) whether the respondent has genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the barriers such that the court should refuse to exercise its powers under
s. 21.1(3)
(c) and (d) of the
Divorce Act
, and (b) if not, the appropriate remedy to be granted.

[
6
]

Ms Sabbah relies on the authority of
H(K) v S(J)
,
2000 Canlii 18733
(QCCS).  In that case the respondent husband relied on what he called his “genuine religious grounds” for refusing to give a “Ghet” (as it was styled in the case). Decarie J relied on the following holding by Tannenbaum J in
Droit de la famille
2296 1:

A married women of the Jewish faith, wherever she may live, who has been divorced by virtue of the civil law cannot, however, remarry according to and in her faith unless she also obtains a release from the religious bonds of marriage. This release referred to as a “Jewish Divorce”, or a “Ghet”, is granted by a Rabbinical court. The Rabbinical court, however, cannot grant the “Ghet” unless the husband consents, if the wife is the party requesting the religious divorce.

It is not too difficult to imagine that the above situation has, over the years, led to many instances where the treat of withholding consent, has forced many woman into accepting unfair agreements with respect to either custody, access, or financial arrangements in the civil divorce.

With respect to people of the Jewish faith, who are divorcing,
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
is a way of leveling the playing field. The Jewish husband who threatens to withhold consent is subject to being denied the right to petition for corollary relief or even a civil divorce itself.

His willingness to grant the “Ghet” only after the civil divorce is completed leads me to conclude that it is his intention to use this power over his wife in settlement negotiations. His offer to consent to the “Ghet” after the civil divorce is meaningless since he would, in no way, be bound to do so.
Section 21.1
, in my view, clearly indicates that the barriers are to be removed prior to the completion of the civil proceedings, since it empowers the Court to dismiss any proceedings taken by the refusing spouse.

On the other hand, agreeing to the “Ghet” prior to completion of the civil divorce would, in no way, prevent the husband from continuing with his proceedings, including his request for custody and the compensatory allowance, etc. and therefore letting the Court decide on these matters based on any evidence that he may tender. (p 730)

[
7
]

In
H(K)

Decarie J concluded the husband’s willingness to give the Ghet only after the civil divorce was completed meant he was using the necessity of his consent to the “Ghet” as “a weapon for negotiations with the Applicant”. As a result, Decarie J struck the husband’s pleadings, but authorized him to refile “if, and only if, his pleadings are accompanied by an affidavit indicating that all of the barriers to Applicant's remarriage in the Jewish religion have been removed, failing which Applicant will be authorized to proceed ex parte”.

[
8
]

The Supreme Court of Canada has considered s 21.1 of the
Divorce Act
, in
Bruker v

Marcovitz
,
2007 SCC 54
. The essence of the decision in
Bruker
is included in the following lengthy but helpful excerpt from Mandeville J’s decision in
S(K) v B(S)
et al,
2015 QCCS 3717
:

[19] In
Bruker
vs Marcovitz,
Justice Abella speaking for the Supreme court explains the objective of this section and why it was adopted by the Legislator. She specifically refers to the Minister’s words at the second reading and to the reading of the amendments as made by the then Minister of Justice, Mrs. Kim Campbell:

[5] For an observant Jewish woman in Canada, this presents a dichotomous scenario: under Canadian law, she is free to divorce her husband regardless of his consent; under Jewish law, however, she remains married to him unless he gives his consent. This means that while she can remarry under Canadian law, she is prevented from remarrying in accordance with her religion. The inability to do so, for many Jewish women, results in the loss of their ability to remarry at all.

[...]

[7]  In response to these concerns, after consultation with the leaders of 50 religious groups in Canada and with the specific agreement of the Roman Catholic, Presbyterian and Anglican churches, in 1990 the then Minister of Justice, Doug Lewis, introduced amendments to the
Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp
.), Bill C-61, giving a court discretionary authority to prevent a spouse from obtaining relief under the Act if that spouse refused to remove a barrier to religious remarriage (
s. 21.1
).  At second reading, the Minister outlined the motivation for these amendments, explaining:

The bill before us today is an amendment to the
Divorce Act
which would provide a court with discretionary powers to preclude a spouse from obtaining relief or proceeding under the Divorce Act where that spouse refuses to remove a barrier to religious remarriage and where the power to remove the barrier to religious remarriage lies solely with that person.  Where the court is satisfied that the spouse who refuses to remove the barrier has genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for doing so, it need not exercise its discretion to grant the remedy provided for in this legislation.

[…]
A spouse should not be able to refuse to participate in a Jewish religious divorce — called a Get — in order to obtain concessions in a civil divorce.  The Get should not be used as a bargaining tool for child custody and access or monetary support.

[…]  I am concerned about protecting the integrity of the
Divorce Act
and preventing persons from avoiding the application of the principles contained in the act.  For example, a wife may feel compelled to agree to custody arrangements which are not truly in the best interests of a couple’s child in order to obtain a Get.

I want to take a few minutes to describe briefly the dilemma certain Jewish persons face because of their religious divorce procedures.  In the Jewish religion divorce is accomplished by the delivery of a Get from the husband and its acceptance by the wife in the presence of a Rabbinical Court.  According to the Jewish religious traditions, the procedure cannot be changed.  Without a Get, a Jewish woman cannot remarry in her own faith.  Children of a subsequent civil marriage suffer religious disabilities.  While difficult remarriage within the Jewish faith for a man in the same circumstances is not impossible.

[...]

[...] the government is moving where it can and where it is brought to the government’s attention to eliminate sexism and gender bias in the law...

[...]

It is the case that in some religions, the Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox and Islam, annulment or divorce may proceed more easily and faster if the couple agree.

However, in all these cases, the authority to grant the annulment or divorce rests with the religious tribunal, not the couple.

An un-co-operative spouse may delay a decision, but ultimately he or she cannot prevent the religious tribunal from rendering its decision.

In these religions, the spouse initiating the action can ask the religious authorities to deal with this problem.

The Jewish spouse does not have that recourse.

(House of Commons Debates, vol. VI, 2nd Sess., 34th Parl., February 15, 1990, at pp. 8375-77)

[8] At third reading of these amendments, Kim Campbell, who succeeded Mr. Lewis as Minister of Justice, confirmed the policy rationale for this legislative initiative:

The purpose of this bill is to assist Jewish citizens whose spouses are withholding a religious divorce, which is called a get, in order to obtain concessions in a civil divorce. [...]

The consequences to women deprived of a get and loyal to their faith are severe. They may not remarry within their faith, even though civilly divorced. If they do remarry, children from a second civil marriage are considered illegitimate and restricted from practising their religion. Such consequences to a religious person leave them open to blackmail from the spouse withholding the get.  For example, the spouse could say, “Give up your claim for support or custody of the children and I will offer the get.” Even those not contemplating a second marriage find it uncomfortable to be considered married within their religion to someone they have divorced civilly.

The vast majority of adherents to the Jewish faith condemn as unfair this practice of bargaining with the get.  Yet they are powerless to amend the situation. Persuasion by rabbis has often proved ineffective.  Since the dispersion of the Jews there is no central Jewish authority to amend the Jewish legal code, [...] which governs the get. Nor is there any modern-day authority within rabbinical courts to enforce the offer and receipt of gets. Full support for Bill C-61 was expressed by major Jewish organizations who attended the hearings before the legislative committee. Representatives of the three Parties praised the bill and quickly passed two minor technical amendments.

As well, the Toronto Board of Orthodox Rabbis [...] endorsed the legislation and the two amendments.

[…]

[Translation]

Bill C-61 will enable Canada’s Jewish community to preserve its traditions without destabilizing models of family life. It also ensures that the principles of the
Divorce Act
with respect to alimony and custody are applied equally to all Canadians.

(House of Commons Debates, vol. VIII, 2nd Sess., 34th Parl., May 4, 1990, at pp. 11033-34)

[9] For many years, civil courts have attempted to remedy, or compensate for, the husband’s recalcitrance in refusing to provide a get to his wife.  They are often faced with assertions by the husband that such interventions are a violation of his freedom of religion.

[…]

[81]
Section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
, which gives a court discretionary authority to rebuff a spouse in civil proceedings who obstructs religious remarriage, is a clear indication that it is public policy in this country that such barriers are to be discouraged.  As the comments of the then Ministers of Justice show, these amendments received overwhelming support from the Jewish community, including its more religious elements, reflecting a consensus that the refusal to provide a get was an unwarranted indignity imposed on Jewish women and, to the extent possible, one that should not be countenanced by Canada’s legal system.

[82]      We also accept the right of Canadians to decide for themselves whether their marriage has irretrievably broken down and we attempt to facilitate, rather than impede, their ability to continue their lives, including with new families. Moreover, under Canadian law, marriage and divorce are available equally to men and women.  A get, on the other hand, can only be given under Jewish law by a husband.  For those Jewish women whose religious principles prevent them from considering remarriage unless they are able to do so in accordance with Jewish law, the denial of a get is the denial of the right to remarry.  It is true that get also requires the consent of the wife, but as Ayelet Shachar points out in Multicultural Jurisdictions, the law has a disparate impact on women:

The family law realm […] vividly illustrates the troubling paradox of multicultural vulnerability, by demonstrating how well-meaning attempts to respect differences often translate into a license for subordination of a particular category of group members — in this instance, primarily women. [p. 62]

The refusal of a husband to provide a get, therefore, arbitrarily denies his wife access to a remedy she independently has under Canadian law and denies her the ability to remarry and get on with her life in accordance with her religious beliefs.

[20]        The Court finds that these comments from the various ministers are quite helpful to understand what are the objectives of the law and how the discretion it provides the courts should be exercised.

[...]

[22] Essentially, all the authorities support the proposition that the legislation granted the courts discretion to intervene where a person withholds consent to give or receive the ghet, because this person may use the ghet as a threat, a leverage tool or a negotiation tool with the effect  that the other spouse who cannot obtain the religious divorce is not able to freely address the Court and advance her rights as she or he wishes.

[
9
]

Turning then to the facts of the case, Mandeville J rejected the respondent husband’s objection that the application under s 21.1 was premature for being interlocutory. Indeed, Mandeville J relied on the Alberta authority of
Darel v Darel
,
1999 ABQB 881
, at para
50
, for the proposition that:

Where the court is of the view that it would be inappropriate to lend its support to a litigant who has improperly withheld a religious divorce, this would constitute a preliminary objection even to the litigant bringing an application for modification of an existing judgment.
[1]

[
10
]

Mandeville J went on to decide that the husband had not performed what was necessary to remove all barriers to a religious marriage and that he had failed to show a genuine ground of a religious or conscientious nature (at paras 54-55).

[
11
]

Bruker v Marcovitz
was also recently considered by Bezaire J in
Zoughaib
v. El-Mokadem
,
2024 ONSC 292
. The court in
Zoughaib

stated:

[
23] Like the majority in
Bruker v. Marcovitz
... I query whether the respondent, in good faith, sincerely objects to removing the barriers as a matter of religious belief or conscience.  Abella J., writing for the majority in Brucker, held:

[68]      … It is not clear to me what aspect of [Mr. Marcovitz’s] religious beliefs prevented him from providing a get [Jewish act of religious divorce].  He never, in fact, offered a religious reason for refusing to provide a get.  Rather, he said that his refusal was based on the fact that, in his words:

Mrs. Bruker harassed me, she alienated my kids from me, she stole some money from me, she stole some silverware from my mother, she prevented my proper visitation with the kids.  Those are the reasons … [Appellant’s Record, at p. 66]

[69] This concession confirms, in my view, that his refusal to provide the get was based less on religious conviction than on the fact that he was angry at Ms. Bruker.  His religion does not require him to refuse to give Ms. Bruker a get.  The contrary is true.  There is no doubt that at Jewish law he could refuse to give one, but that is very different from Mr. Marcovitz being prevented by a tenet of his religious beliefs from complying with a legal obligation he voluntarily entered into and of which he took the negotiated benefits. [Emphasis in original].

[24] The same situation exists here. It is not clear to me what aspect of the respondent’s religious beliefs prevent him from providing talaq.  During oral testimony, the respondent admitted that his religion allows him to consent to talaq.  He also admitted that he has so consented twice before, following his two prior marriages.  The fact that Sharia Law allows him to withhold his consent does not equate to him being prevented from doing so by any genuine religious or conscientious belief.

[
12
]

In
Zoughaib

Bezaire J. considered the husband’s evidence regarding his genuine religious or conscientious belief arising under Sharia law but did not find it credible. She concluded his reliance was “unclear... as to how the civil legal resolution failed to accord with Sharia Law or how granting
talaq
would be the equivalent of renouncing he religious authority of Sharia. Further, no expert evidence was tendered on the motion”. (at para 21) Bezaire J went on to conclude that on the entire record before her,
“[t]he grounds presented for refusing consent have less to do with genuine religious belief and more to do with the fact the respondent is angry with the applicant for suing him in this Court”. (at para 32)

Application of the law to the facts of this case

[
13
]

As noted in the Concise letter filed on behalf of Mr. Sabbah, s 21.1(3) was introduced to prevent a husband from using the Get to negotiate a better deal for himself through coercion during divorce proceedings. Counsel helpfully acknowledges that the law also balances the interests of the parties.
Section 21.1(4)
(a) of the
Divorce Act
provides that a husband, in response to a spouse’s application to strike pleadings and the like, may provide “genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the barriers referred to in
paragraph 2
(e).

[
14
]

Here, in his affidavits sworn March 15, 2024 and June 11, 2024 Mr. Sabbah deposes several such grounds.

[
15
]

In his March 15, 2024 affidavit, he deposes that in his religion, a party committing adultery – which he alleges against Ms Sabbah – “walks away from the marriage with no share of the property, and in addition there are other religious penalties” (at para 14). Elsewhere in the same affidavit, however, he allows that in his understanding of Judaism, civil laws take priority over religious laws, which is why he says he is willing to resolve property issues on an equal basis. He then says:

I am willing to grant the Get, but only after we have been granted a divorce civilly. I do not want to be civilly married to [Ms. Sabbah] not divorce religiously [sic]. This makes no sense to me. (at para 17)

[
16
]

Nowhere in his March 15, 2024 affidavit does Mr. Sabbah say that his position regarding the Get is based on genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature.

[
17
]

On the other hand, he does raise such grounds in his subsequent June 11, 2024 affidavit. By that time Mr. Sabbah had been served with Ms. Sabbah’s application relying on s 21.1 of the
Divorce Act
. (His prior March 15, 2024 affidavit addressed the Get in the context of answering Ms. Sabbah’s own February 29, 2024 affidavit. Ms Sabbah’s affidavit certainly raised issues with the Get, but not specifically with a s 21.1
Divorce Act
application on the table.)

[
18
]

In his June 11, 2024 affidavit Mr. Sabbah further deposes that:

-

His conscientious and deeply held religious beliefs cannot allow him to grant his wife a religious divorce until the time that he is civilly divorced from his wife. Granting his wife a religious divorce prior to a civil divorce is contrary to his faith;

-

A Get is only a barrier to an observant Jewish woman in the orthodox faith. Mr. Sabbah contends that his wife is not “an observant Jewish woman”. As such, Mr. Sabbah “cannot in good conscience, according to his deeply held religious beliefs, consent to a religious divorce while he is still married to Ms Sabbah. If he were to do so, he would be in direct contravention off the law of Moses, specifically the book of Exodus 20:12 (including the Ten Commandments), and the book of Deuteronomy 6:7, 6:9, and 24:2. Mr. Sabbah says it would be unconscionable for him to divorce his wife religiously before divorcing her civilly, as remaining civilly married yet religiously divorced is prohibited under Jewish law;

-

Again, however in relation to the alleged adultery, Mr. Sabbah cites the books Maimonides in Mishnei Torah, Sefer Nashim, Ishut, chapter 24, and repeats that the “abomination” of adultery engaged in by Ms Sabbah prohibits him from divorcing Ms. Sabbah religiously, especially if he is then to acknowledge her in public and religious as civilly married.

[
19
]

At Exhibit C of his June 11, 2024 affidavit Mr. Sabbah excerpts the above-mentioned passages from Deuteronomy and Exodus. These passages appear to speak particularly to the question of “adultery” in certain circumstances. That being said, the court is no expert on the law of Mr. Sabbah’s faith, and no independent expert evidence is before me on how these passages inform the law of Mr. Sabbah’s faith regarding the giving of a Get. This is not to say that expert evidence will always be necessary in cases like this. It is worth asking if the rules governing proof of foreign law apply. I am reluctant to say more however if only because the matter was not argued before me. Except to note that courts have found such evidence helpful:
DN v BN
,
2022 BCSC 2029
, and as I am doing, have noted its absence:
Zoughaib v. El-Mokadem
,
2024 ONSC 292
.

[
20
]

Expert evidence aside, Mr. Sabbah also brings nothing before the court to assist in the independent interpretation of the passages he refers to. As I review those passages, it is enough to say that in the context of s 21.1 of the
Divorce Act
they do not speak for themselves. Nothing else is before me that sets out independently what Mr. Sabbah says is the law of his faith on these questions. Put another way, whatever Mr. Sabbah says subjectively about the passages and how they inform him as to the law of this faith, I have nothing else that informs me as to the objective validity of his statements. On the whole, Mr. Sabbah has brought forward little that persuades me his ’genuine religious beliefs’ are but subjectively binding on him.

[
21
]

I then consider, as the court did in
Zoughaib
, if “[t]he grounds presented for refusing consent have less to do with genuine religious belief and more to do with the fact the respondent is angry with the applicant for suing him in this Court” (at para 32). The uncontroverted and frankly very damaging evidence in this case is of Mr. Sabbah using his ability to withhold consent to the Get as a bargaining tool in the civil divorce proceedings.

[
22
]

Through counsel and as set out at TAB F in her affidavit filed March 1, 2024, Ms Sabbah points to what I agree are examples of ‘leveraging’ the Get in the civil proceedings:

-

That he has indicated that the Get will be getting more expensive as time goes by, that “I may die never signing your get”, and until Ms Sabbah pays certain of his legal fees, she’s “getting shit” from him (Exhibit I)

-

That “I am adding $1,000 to the get for pain and suffering” for each time Ms. Sabbah’s now-partner picks up the children (Exh J)

-

That if Ms Sabbah wants the Get, she needs to walk away, and the more times she takes Mr. Sabbah to court for no reason, the more her Get will cost, and it doesn’t bother him if the price becomes out of reach (Exh K)

-

“When your family and yourself pay back the money I burned believing your lies, when it was obvious you were truing to manipulate me, we can sign the ghet. An adulteress gets zero according to Jewish law, so anything you steal in the meantime through courts will only make the ghet more expensive for you to receive. Even if this means I’ll never be able to sign a ghet, it is only you who can fix this.” (Exh L)

-

Even in correspondence to a third party Rabbi dated March 14, 2024, Mr. Sabbah has stated that “The more she costs me in civil court trying to get money she is not entitled to, the more the get will cost before I am able to sign it.” (TAB G, Exh G)

[
23
]

Mr. Sabbah swore his own June 11, 2024 affidavit “to update the Court on matters which have occurred since my last Affidavit was filed”. Mr. Sabbah’s earlier affidavit was filed March 15, 2024. In neither affidavit does Mr. Sabbah deny or even address the alleged ‘leveraging’ correspondence noted above. In all of his evidence, the message is clear that he is willing to give the Get but only “provided it [is] bundled with a conclusion of the civil divorce proceedings”. (para 3)

Conclusion

[
24
]

For the reasons given the application is allowed.

[
25
]

As to specific relief, while no existing or new applications will be allowed to proceed or be initiated, the actual striking of pleadings will be abeyanced until February 14, 2025, to allow Mr. Sabbah to file an affidavit indicating that all barriers to a Religious Divorce have been removed per
s. 21.1(2)
of the
Divorce Act
, failing which Mr. Sabbah’s pleadings and affidavits shall be immediately struck and Mr. Sabbah will be unable to further participate in these proceedings.

Costs

[
26
]

Ms Sabbah seeks significantly enhanced costs. I am not persuaded that this case is like that case relied on of
DN v BN
,
2022 BCSC 2029
. No other authority was argued, or has come to my attention, to justify an award of costs other than is provided by Schedule C, Column One, of the Rules of Court.

Heard on the
28
th
day of June, 2024.

Dated
at Edmonton, Alberta this
18
th
day of December, 2024.

Peter Michalyshyn

J.C.K.B.A.

Appearances:

Kathryn A. McNeil

Liddell Law Office

for the Applicant

Spencer P. Morrison

Morrison Law

for the Respondent

[1]
To a similar effect,
Sablani v Sablani
,
2023 ONSC 6288
, at para
14
. Counsel for Mr.. Sabbah objects that none of the authorities relied on by the applicant deal with interlocutory applications. I agree with counsel for Ms. Sabbah that ample authority justifies the intervention of the court at the interlocutory stage of a proceeding:
S(K) v B(S) et al
,
2015 QCCS 3717
, and like authorities mentioned elsewhere in this decision.
